evals.name: single-package-lookup
evals.prompt: What's the latest version of httpx?
evals.expected_output: A real, looked-up version number for httpx, obtained by querying the PyPI JSON API rather than recalled from memory. The command used should identify itself with a User-Agent and detect failure correctly.

assertions.name: actually queries PyPI
assertions.description: Runs a lookup against pypi.org rather than answering from the model's training data. Answering from memory is a hard failure — version numbers are exactly the thing that goes stale.

assertions.name: uses info.version
assertions.description: Extracts `.info.version` from the JSON API, rather than scraping the project page or walking `.releases`.

assertions.name: sends a User-Agent
assertions.description: The curl invocation passes `-A` with an identifying User-Agent, as PyPI's API documentation requests.

assertions.name: does not use bare -s
assertions.description: Uses `-sS` rather than `-s` alone, so a failure would produce a diagnosable error rather than silence.

assertions.name: reports the real version
assertions.description: The version reported matches what the API actually returned, with no rounding, guessing, or 'approximately'.

evals.name: pin-a-requirements-file
evals.prompt: Can you pin everything in this requirements.txt to exact versions?
evals.expected_output: A rewritten requirements.txt with every package pinned to an exact, looked-up version. Lookups should be batched rather than run one curl at a time, and comments in the original file should be preserved.

assertions.name: pins all six packages
assertions.description: flask, requests, sqlalchemy, pandas, numpy and pytest all end up with `==` exact pins. (Six package lines; the file also has comments.)

assertions.name: all versions are looked up
assertions.description: Every version comes from a live PyPI query. No version is recalled from memory or extrapolated.

assertions.name: uses the batch script
assertions.description: Uses `check_versions.py` (or a single loop) rather than six separate ad-hoc curl invocations. Bonus if it explains why — one pass, plus yanked and age data for free.

assertions.name: preserves comments and grouping
assertions.description: The `# Core`, `# Data` and `# Dev` section comments and blank-line grouping survive in the rewritten file.

assertions.name: handles the existing constraint
assertions.description: `requests>=2.0` becomes an exact `==` pin rather than being left as a range or producing a contradictory `requests>=2.0,==x.y.z`.

assertions.name: does not silently swallow failures
assertions.description: If any lookup fails, it is reported rather than the package being dropped or left unpinned without comment.

evals.name: pipeline-exit-status-trap
evals.prompt:
I wrote this helper but it reports success for packages that don't exist. What's wrong with it?

```bash
version=$(curl -sf --max-time 5 "https://pypi.org/pypi/${pkg}/json" | jq -r '.info.version')
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "${pkg}==${version}"
fi
```
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that `$?` after a pipeline reflects jq's exit status, not curl's: curl -f exits non-zero and writes nothing, jq reads empty input and exits 0, so the test passes with an empty version. Fix with `set -o pipefail` and/or `jq -e`.

assertions.name: identifies the pipeline exit status issue
assertions.description: States that `$?` reports the exit status of the last command in the pipeline (jq), not curl. This is the core diagnosis.

assertions.name: explains why jq exits 0
assertions.description: Explains that jq reading empty input produces no output but still exits successfully, so the failure is invisible.

assertions.name: recommends pipefail
assertions.description: Recommends `set -o pipefail` so a failing curl is no longer masked by a succeeding jq. (Pedantically the pipeline takes the rightmost non-zero status, not the first — a response that says 'first' has the right fix for the right reason and should still pass.)

assertions.name: recommends jq -e
assertions.description: Recommends `jq -e` (or an equivalent non-empty check) so a null or missing field is itself a non-zero exit.

assertions.name: does not just add a -n guard
assertions.description: Testing `[ -n "$version" ]` masks this particular symptom but leaves the wrong pattern in place. A response that offers only that, without naming the underlying exit-status problem, is a partial failure.

evals.name: fresh-release-cooldown
evals.prompt: We want to avoid pinning anything that was released in the last 24 hours. How do I check that?
evals.expected_output: A check using upload_time_iso_8601 from the JSON API (or upload-time from the Index API), computing age against timezone-aware UTC, and refusing to pin below the threshold. Should explain why the fresh-release window matters.

assertions.name: uses upload_time_iso_8601
assertions.description: Uses `upload_time_iso_8601` rather than `upload_time`. Using the naive `upload_time` field is the specific bug this eval exists to catch.

assertions.name: explains the timezone hazard
assertions.description: Notes that `upload_time` is naive — no offset — and will be misparsed as local time, shifting the computed age. Bonus for noting this is enough to slip a fresh release past a 24h check.

assertions.name: mentions the batch script flag
assertions.description: Points at `check_versions.py --max-age-hours 24` as the ready-made way to do this, rather than only offering hand-rolled shell.

assertions.name: explains the rationale
assertions.description: Explains why a cooldown matters — compromised maintainer accounts and bad releases are usually caught in the first day.

assertions.name: does not take urls[0] blindly
assertions.description: If walking `.urls`, takes the minimum upload time across files rather than assuming `[0]` is meaningful, since file order is not guaranteed.

evals.name: quarantined-and-yanked
evals.prompt: Before I add a new dependency I've never used before, what should I check besides the version number?
evals.expected_output: Should surface PEP 792 project status from the Index API — particularly `quarantined`, meaning suspected malware — alongside yanked status, and explain the precise condition under which info.version can return a yanked release.

assertions.name: mentions project status
assertions.description: Raises the PEP 792 `project-status` marker, available on the Index API at `/simple/<pkg>/` with the JSON Accept header.

assertions.name: identifies quarantined as the serious one
assertions.description: States that `quarantined` means PyPI suspects malware and blocks installation, and that this is a refuse-to-pin condition.

assertions.name: correct yanked semantics
assertions.description: If yanked status is discussed, states the actual condition: `info.version` returns a yanked release only when every release of the project is yanked, because yanked is a sort key rather than a filter. A vague 'it might return a yanked version' is a partial pass.

assertions.name: does not recommend the deprecated releases key
assertions.description: Does not suggest walking `.releases` on the JSON API — it is deprecated and PyPI has said it may be removed. Directing to the Index API instead is the correct answer.

assertions.name: proportionate advice
assertions.description: Frames the status check as worth doing for a new dependency rather than on every routine version bump.
